clue.text: It's a job being sober daily, perhaps …

parts.note: someone sober is dry, off the drink
a daily is a British term for a cleaner who comes in each day

explanation.surface: A recovering drinker reflects that staying sober every single day is hard work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'daily' looks like 'every day' but is a noun: in Britain a daily is a domestic cleaner.
explanation.definitionFit: Laundering clothes with solvents is an occupation, so the trade is fairly called a job.

clue.text: Flipping good day to get very drunk

indicators.note: flipping means turning over, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: pi is short for pious, meaning good
so means very, as in 'so tired'

explanation.surface: A grumble about a perfectly good day ending in heavy drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' sounds like a mild curse but reverses PI to IP.
explanation.definitionFit: A dipso is a habitual heavy drinker, the noun sense of the clue word.

clue.text: Old Russian boozer in style after refurbishment

indicators.note: a refurbishment rebuilds something, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A refurbished pub with a stylish old Russian theme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boozer' suggests a British pub but is a heavy drinker here.
explanation.definitionFit: Boris Yeltsin, the first post-Soviet president, was notorious for drinking heavily.

clue.text: Stay relations cracking drink makes merry

parts.note: to live somewhere is to stay there

indicators.note: cracking means breaking into, so these letters get split by others

parts.note: to sup is to drink
it is slang for sex, and sexual relations

explanation.surface: Visiting relatives cracking open drinks and partying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'relations' looks like family but is sex, slangily IT; 'cracking' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: To celebrate extravagantly and have a riotous time is to party, the same as making merry.

clue.text: What might cause one to throw up in Dakota?

definitions.text: What might cause one to throw up in Dakota?

parts.words: What might cause one to throw up in Dakota?
parts.note: the Douglas Dakota is a well-known aircraft, not only the US states

explanation.surface: Something that makes travellers vomit in the American Dakotas.
explanation.walkthrough: Dakota looks like a US state; it is the Douglas DC-3 aeroplane.
explanation.definitionFit: Nausea from flying turbulence can make a passenger vomit aboard a plane.

clue.text: I love getting to the end of the case of eggnog

indicators.note: getting to the end means one piece goes after the other
the case of a word is its outside, its first and final letters

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, so O

explanation.surface: Someone declaring their fondness for draining the last of the eggnog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I' looks like the speaker but is the definition: the self.
explanation.definitionFit: In psychology the self or 'I' is a person's sense of identity.

clue.text: … because I must neck Tesco's top wine

indicators.note: to neck a drink is to swallow it, so these letters take another one inside them

parts.note: as can mean because, as in 'as it was late'

indicators.note: the top of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Continuing the drinker's excuses: the supermarket's best wine simply has to be gulped down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'must neck' puts T, the first letter of Tesco's (a UK supermarket chain), inside AS + I.
explanation.definitionFit: Asti is a sparkling Italian vintage from Piedmont, an example of the drink.

clue.text: A poem Stein drunkenly set in South Africa

indicators.note: set in means placed inside, so the jumbled letters go within others
drunkenly means the letters stagger into a new order

explanation.surface: Gertrude Stein wrote a drunken poem with a South African setting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunkenly' rearranges STEIN to ESTIN.
explanation.definitionFit: A sestina is a verse form of six stanzas with repeating end words.

clue.text: Hypocritical as half-cut Reed supporting early-closing pub?

indicators.note: in a down clue, supporting means placed below
closing early means the end is cut off

parts.note: an inn is a pub
as can mean since, as in 'as you asked'

indicators.note: half-cut means only the first half of the word is kept

explanation.surface: A tipsy man named Reed backs a pub that shuts early, an act of hypocrisy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half-cut' means drunk but here keeps RE; 'early-closing' cuts INN to IN.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone hypocritical says what they do not mean, pretending to feelings they lack.

clue.text: Britons on vacation drinking like fishes

indicators.note: drinking means taking in, so these letters go inside
vacated means emptied, so only the outer letters remain

parts.note: as means like, as in 'white as snow'

explanation.surface: British holidaymakers drinking like fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on vacation' empties a word, keeping only its outer letters; 'drinking' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: This perch-like species is a type of fish, and its plural is often the same form.

clue.text: Vicar with a drink going about tedious business

indicators.note: to go about is to turn around, so the whole string is read backwards

parts.note: Rev is the short title of a clergyman
to lap is to drink as a cat does

explanation.surface: A clergyman with a pint makes a tiresome fuss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going about' reverses REV + A + LAP (REVALAP).
explanation.definitionFit: Palaver is wearisome fuss and bother, a laborious procedure or rigmarole.

clue.text: Tipsy idiot Hoskins finally snogs head of fleet?

parts.note: a bit on is slang for slightly drunk
an ass is a fool
Hoskins is the setter, who refers to himself as I

indicators.note: finally picks the last letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: A drunk crossword setter kisses the admiral in charge of the ships.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's name stands for I, a common crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: Aristotle Onassis was a Greek shipping tycoon, master of a great merchant fleet.

clue.text: Old relation drinking in a watering hole?

parts.note: sis is short for sister, a relation

explanation.surface: An elderly relative boozing at a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'watering hole' usually means a pub; here it is a literal water source.
explanation.definitionFit: A desert spring where travellers and animals drink is literally a place for watering.

clue.text: Not on vacation, but at home having booze-up

parts.note: in means at home, as in 'staying in'
a session is British slang for a long drinking bout

explanation.surface: Someone skipped the holiday to stay home and drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Courts and parliaments are sitting, not in recess, when the body is formally meeting.

clue.text: Private chap after a Martini drinker's job?

indicators.note: after means the piece comes later in the word

parts.note: secret means private
a gent is a chap

explanation.surface: A private man's ambitions to a cocktail-swilling lifestyle.
explanation.walkthrough: James Bond famously drinks Martinis.
explanation.definitionFit: Spying is the profession of James Bond, the most famous Martini drinker in fiction.

clue.text: Something roaring inebriates have put away?

definitions.text: Something roaring inebriates have put away?

indicators.note: putting something away is storing it out of sight, so the letters sit concealed in the words before

explanation.surface: What noisy drunks have downed.
explanation.walkthrough: To put away is also to drink, so the whole clue doubles as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Raucous drunks may have knocked back a juniper spirit, the classic tipple for the purpose.

clue.text: Hoist keg up over liquid resembling spirits

indicators.note: over means covering, so the jumbled letters surround another
up means stirred up or in disarray, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: L is the chemistry state symbol for a liquid

explanation.surface: Lifting a beer barrel over spilt liquid, as hard as hauling liquor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' rearranges HOISTKEG to GHOSTIKE, which goes round L.
explanation.definitionFit: Spirits here are ghosts, so the answer means phantom-like or spectral.

clue.text: What a beer thief might do to be brave in adversity

definitions.text: What a beer thief might do
definitions.meaning: Courage is a British brewery whose beer a thief could steal
to find nerve when facing trouble

explanation.surface: A beer thief's habit is also a lesson in bravery.
explanation.walkthrough: Courage is a long-established English beer brand.
explanation.definitionFit: Summoning boldness when facing danger; the same phrase is literally stealing the beer.

clue.text: He put in a new order ahead of bum due a tot?

indicators.note: ahead of means the anagram comes first
putting things in a new order rearranges them

parts.note: bum and duff are both slang for worthless

explanation.surface: A man rearranges his order at the bar ahead of a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tot' looks like a measure of spirits but is a small child. UP THE DUFF is British slang for pregnant.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone expecting a baby is pregnant, here slangily said to be due a child.

clue.text: Squiffy on mere pints, yet all over the place?

indicators.note: squiffy means tipsy, so the letters stagger into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone already drunk on only a few pints, staggering around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all over the place' sounds like confusion but means everywhere.
explanation.definitionFit: Being everywhere at once is literally being present throughout every location.

clue.text: Developing centre for wines with one bouquet?

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle letter

parts.note: a means one
a wine's bouquet is its scent

explanation.surface: A wine shop chooses its middle range of bottles for their bouquet.
explanation.definitionFit: Something nascent is just coming into being, still forming and growing.

clue.text: US college girl not initially drunk as a Lord?

indicators.note: not means the letter after it is left out

parts.note: a coed is an American term for a female student

indicators.note: initially picks the first letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: An American student who's sober compared to a peer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as' is only a link; 'drunk as a lord' is a red herring idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: Sebastian Coe, the athlete and Olympics organiser, sits in the House of Lords as a life peer.

clue.text: Two containers of beer on a bar in Mexico?

parts.note: beer comes in a can and in a tin, two containers

explanation.surface: Two beers in cans on a counter in a Mexican bar.
explanation.definitionFit: A cantina is the Spanish word for a tavern or saloon in Mexico.

clue.text: Drunken Ant a mess, having a drink down under

indicators.note: drunken means the letters reel into a new order

explanation.surface: A man called Ant is in a state, still clutching a drink, in Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunken' rearranges ANT A MESS (giving TASMANSE); the A of 'having a' follows. 'drink' is slang for the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: The drink is slang for sea, and this stretch of water lies between Australia and New Zealand.

clue.text: A smart sort of chap putting beer on tap

parts.note: ale is a beer
C marks the cold tap

explanation.surface: A dapper man pulling a beer at the tap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'smart alec' is a know-all; the definition hides the name inside the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A know-all is called a smart Alec, so the name fills the gap.

clue.text: 2012 Olympian game to polish off last of Merlot

indicators.note: to polish off is to finish or get rid of, so a letter is removed

parts.note: tennis is a game

indicators.note: last of picks the final letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: A sporting contest to see off what remains of the red wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Jessica Ennis won heptathlon gold for Britain at the London Games of that year.

clue.text: An explosive market a drunkard mentions

indicators.note: a slurring drunk turns the s sound into sh

parts.note: to market goods is to sell them

explanation.surface: A drunk talks about a market rigged to explode.
explanation.walkthrough: Slurred speech turns S into SH.
explanation.definitionFit: An artillery projectile with a bursting charge is an explosive missile.

clue.text: A drink of lager on the rocks?

indicators.note: in an across clue, one piece on another follows it

parts.note: on the rocks means served over ice, so the rocks are ice
lager is a beer

explanation.surface: Asking for a lager served over ice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the rocks' reads as a whole phrase, but 'on' joins the pieces and 'the rocks' alone is ICE.
explanation.definitionFit: This strong lager style is made by freezing the brew, a kind of beverage.

clue.text: Half-cut England captain and Aussie skipper

indicators.note: half-cut keeps only the first half of the word

parts.note: Wayne Rooney captained the England football team

explanation.surface: A drunken England football captain alongside the Australian cricket captain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'skipper' looks like a captain but is something that hops: a kangaroo.
explanation.definitionFit: Kangaroos hop, so they skip; Australian slang shortens the animal's name.

clue.text: Slippery nipple cocktail you bypass at last topless club that's seedy

indicators.note: at last picks the final letter of each of the words before it
topless means the first letter is taken off

parts.note: a dive is a seedy nightclub or bar

explanation.surface: A cocktail bar story: a Slippery Nipple drink, a tawdry topless club you'd rather avoid.
explanation.walkthrough: A Slippery Nipple is a real cocktail, so 'Slippery' looks part of its name. 'topless' drops D from DIVE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something evasive and hard to catch hold of is slippery in the figurative sense.

clue.text: Time to go back for brews and some food

indicators.note: go back means the letter shifts further along the word

parts.note: teas are brews in British slang

explanation.surface: Time to head home for tea and a bite to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to go back' moves T in TEAS further back.
explanation.definitionFit: Eats is informal slang for meals or snacks.

clue.text: A boozer on a nautical-themed pub crawl?

definitions.text: A boozer on a nautical-themed pub crawl?

parts.words: A boozer on a nautical-themed pub crawl?
parts.note: a pub crawl visits pubs in turn; with a seafaring theme each one becomes a harbour stop

explanation.surface: Drinkers touring pubs dressed as sailors.
explanation.definitionFit: A harbour where a ship stops on its voyage, and also any place one regularly visits.
